sources.entry: pyinstrument - A statistical wall-clock profiler with low overhead and readable call-tree output.

summary.one_liner: pyinstrument is a Python statistical profiler that samples call stacks and shows where wall-clock time goes in a readable call tree.
summary.what_it_does: Pyinstrument samples a running Python program and records the call stack, so you can see which functions take the most time. It prints a call-tree readout to the console by default and can also render HTML reports, JSON, pstats files, speedscope files, and saved sessions. It can be used from the command line (`pyinstrument script.py`, `-m module`, `-c code`), or from code via a Profiler object, a `with` block, or a decorator. It also has an IPython/Jupyter `%%pyinstrument` magic and a Django middleware. Async code is handled by tracking time spent awaiting inside tasks, and output can be filtered to hide library frames or show a flat list of functions.
use_cases: find the slow part of a Python program
profile a script from the command line
profile a Django request or view
profile code in a Jupyter notebook cell
generate an interactive HTML profile report
compare call times with speedscope flame charts
notable: Statistical sampling profiler with low overhead and no main-thread restriction
Async-aware: shows time spent under an await as an [await] node
Interactive HTML output with timeline mode and collapsible call tree
Hides library frames by default, based on Python install and virtualenv paths
Multiple output formats including speedscope and pstats
caveats: Profiling inside Docker containers can give odd results because of slow gettimeofday syscalls (issue #83)
Pickled classes in scripts run via `pyinstrument script.py` may fail because __main__ is not found
Running from a git checkout requires a build step
